Before each interaction, participants were informed whether the VH was human- or computer-controlled, matching the actual controller at the beginning, but were unaware of possible control transitions. We found that perceived agency was strongly influenced by the controller presented at the beginning of the interaction, with no evidence of updating following the control transitions. Social evaluations including likeability and co-presence were generally higher in conditions where human control occurred later and covered a greater proportion of the interaction. The results suggest that prior beliefs and first impressions continued to shape perceived agency, whereas social evaluations were more sens

ea8cbc1bdc4f891a6b1341b9.title_original: A Strict Upper Bound for Three-Point Weighted Selection in Planar Vector-Valued Regression
ea8cbc1bdc4f891a6b1341b9.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12550v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove $F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)<11/6$ for minimum-Frobenius-norm least-squares regression with two input and two output coordinates, improving the upper bound $15/8$. More precisely, a universal $\varepsilon_0>0$ satisfies $\mathcal T_3\le(5/6-\varepsilon_0)E$ for every finite residual frame. The proof combines an exact scalar certificate, rigidity of equality in planar selection, and a compactness argument that controls disappearing weights. Together with the known lower bound, this gives $13/8\le F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)<11/6$. No numerical value of $\varepsilon_0$ is claimed.

440f4e22cc0709707c08f07f.title_original: WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?
440f4e22cc0709707c08f07f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12557v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3-25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.

4930e7d6daa6e965293e7668.title_original: AgentOPSD: Turn-Level Credit Assignment via Recursive Belief Revision
4930e7d6daa6e965293e7668.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12587v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards ordinarily spreads a single advantage over a whole trajectory, a granularity too coarse to isolate the few decisions on which success in a long, multi-turn interaction actually turns. Privileged self-distillation supplies denser supervision, but it leaves unanswered how a set of local teacher-student discrepancies should be converted into credit along a sequence. We introduce AgentOPSD, a critic-free scheme that assigns credit recursively, one interaction turn at a time. Inside a turn, the token-level log-probability gaps between a skill-conditioned self-teacher and the student are summed, and that sum acts as evidence in a recursive Bayesian update carried out in log-odds space; the resulting revisions reallocate the outcome-derived advantage across turns through a multiplier that is bounded and preserves its sign. With Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B as policy backbones on ALFWorld, the method improves consistently on GRPO and on self-distillation baselines, and attains 89.1% success at the 7B scale. Ablations attribute the gain to aggregating evidence at turn boundaries and to making the belief revision depend on history, rather than to the local gap by itself.

32fbe98c47848e12048c5a04.title_original: Unmasking Four Knapsack Problems in the Traveling Thief Benchmark
32fbe98c47848e12048c5a04.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12597v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The traveling thief problem (TTP) asks a thief to choose a tour and a packing together, and the benchmark of 9,720 instances of Polyakovskiy et al. (2014) is the standard test set for comparing TTP heuristics. We show that four of these instances are not TTP instances at all. Their files give a renting rate of 0.00, so the tour has no effect on the objective and each instance reduces to a 0-1 knapsack problem. One of them belongs to the 60 categorized instances on which new methods are usually compared, and on it five of nine published methods report exactly the same value. The cause is the format of the files, which keep the renting rate with two decimals, while the rule of the generator gives a rate close to 0.003 on these instances. The same rounding may shift the rate of 949 other instances by more than 1%. Since the tour and the packing used by the generator were not published, the original rates cannot be recovered. We therefore define new rates with the same rule, applied to a fully specified reference solution that we publish, and we show with a published heuristic that the corrected instances behave as TTP instances again. We also give reference results on the corrected instances and recommendations for future studies. Finally, we present ttplib, a new open-source Python library that loads any of the 9,720 instances, including the corrected ones, without downloading the whole benchmark.

7c2acc5e51378a6a854fcad1.title_original: Double Blind Evals: Resolving the Dual Confidentiality Dilemma in AI Safety Auditing
7c2acc5e51378a6a854fcad1.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12604v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI safety evaluations often involve sensitive prompts and proprietary models. Evaluators want to keep their evaluation prompts secret from model owners to prevent purposeful or incidental data leakage, ensuring longer usefulness of their benchmark. Model owners in turn wish to keep their proprietary model weights and inference code within their own secure infrastructure to protect their IP. We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. To accomplish this, we use secure enclaves that encrypt data in RAM at the hardware level. In a world-first pilot, we test this approach by evaluating a proprietary Google DeepMind model (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) against a selection of the private AILuminate benchmark corpus, using an NVIDIA H100 secure enclave on Google Cloud Platform, and using OpenMined's PySyft to maintain data and model privacy. We believe this effort marks the first use of this technology to provide mutual secrecy for one organization's frontier-class proprietary model weights and another organization's closed benchmark.

f315ffc30359129daaf6d014.title_original: Adapting Small Language Models to Romanized Nepali: Tokenizer Fertility, Reference Likelihood, and Generation Metrics
f315ffc30359129daaf6d014.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12628v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Romanized Nepali, Nepali written in Latin script, is common in digital communication but has no standard spelling and few resources, and it is unclear how reliably small open language models can be adapted to it. We adapt three 2-3B base models from different families, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Gemma-2-2B, with QLoRA on 9,000 instruction examples produced by deterministic transliteration of Nepali instruction data. Each model is trained with one shared recipe and three seeds and evaluated on 1,000 held-out examples with reference-overlap metrics, byte-normalized reference likelihood (bits per byte, BPB), and an output audit, against zero-shot baselines under two prompts. Fine-tuning raises chrF++ from 10-14 to 29.0-30.6 and lowers BPB from 2.23-2.41 to 0.78-0.84; most zero-shot outputs (54-92%) are English-like. Likelihood and overlap disagree on how far apart the models are. Llama-3.2-3B has the lowest BPB in every seed, 0.042 below Qwen2.5-3B (95% CI 0.039-0.046), yet the two cannot be separated on chrF++ (30.51 and 30.61) or BLEU, even with paired item-level tests. Gemma-2-2B, whose tokenizer splits Romanized Nepali words least (2.72 tokens per word), scores worst on every measure. Which model gains most over its zero-shot baseline depends on the zero-shot prompt. In a supplementary comparison with an identical tokenizer, Llama-3.1-8B lowers BPB by 0.053 (0.050-0.056) relative to Llama-3.2-3B, while chrF++ and BLEU rise

4b1912d7519ace620d6b4613.title_original: Certify, Report, or Refuse: Harm-Constrained Conformal Prediction for Clinical Actions
4b1912d7519ace620d6b4613.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12662v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Routing a melanoma case to routine follow-up is a serious action error that diagnostic coverage alone does not rule out. We present Harm-Constrained Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction (HC-ROCP), a training-free framework that uses frozen classifier probabilities and adds a harm penalty when choosing prediction sets and actions. We test the resulting policies on disjoint calibration splits with multiplicity adjustment. HC-ROCP certifies supported claims, reports descriptive fallback policies, and refuses unsupported subgroup claims. We evaluate these outputs retrospectively on COVID-19 radiographs, ISIC 2019 dermoscopy, and EyePACS-to-APTOS retinopathy transfer. Across ten calibration seeds, HC-ROCP reduces COVID-19 severe-action errors from the exact risk-optimal baseline's 4.68\% to 0.54\%. At a 5\% budget, global claims are certified for COVID-19 and ISIC, but the rare squamous-cell-carcinoma claim is refused. At 1\%, all settings receive descriptive reports. For each budget, we also report the minimum severe-case count needed to pass the global harm gate with zero errors, providing a starting point for further data collection.

6db1e4a24287b91093f42f19.title_original: Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model
6db1e4a24287b91093f42f19.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12678v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.

188417066934c3044bbe587d.title_original: reComposer: Editable Planning for Controllable Image Generation
188417066934c3044bbe587d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12687v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Prompt-based image generation makes it easy to produce visual assets, but offers little support for engaging with the creative process. Prompting collapses interdependent creative decisions into a monolithic instruction and returns a finished image, leaving control limited to revising the prompt or correcting the model's output. We present reComposer, a process-oriented image-generation interface built around editable planning, which decomposes users' evolving intent into meaningful creative decisions - such as subject, composition, or palette - and collaborates with users to explore underspecified goals and alternatives. reComposer supports conversational and direct manipulation of the plan, moving between concept-level intent and visual-level control. We evaluated reComposer with 8 design and non-design professionals. Compared to prompting, participants felt greater control and ownership while developing visual assets, exploring alternatives, and iterating on details. Our findings suggest how shifting generative AI interaction from specifying outputs to shaping process can support creative thinking alongside asset production.

268cda589d3468a60c97e87d.title_original: GeoScope: Training-Free Program Execution beyond the Counting Horizon for Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Question Answering
268cda589d3468a60c97e87d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12699v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing images, the objects that questions count in a region or relate by direction often span only a few pixels. Existing methods mainly decide where a vision-language model (VLM) should look and trust its answer in the chosen view. We show that this assumption fails for counting, and measure VLMs as one calibrates a sensor. All eight open VLMs tested fall increasingly short once a view holds more than a certain number of objects, about five for most on DOTA aerial images. This counting horizon narrows as views grow and objects appear smaller. An empirical power-law response model predicts the undercount a split recovers and the spurious counts it adds, and supports the rule of splitting only views beyond the horizon. In GeoScope, a text-only language model parses the question into a typed spatial program that fixes the region and its resolution. The VLM only grounds and counts within its operating range, and directions are computed explicitly from the grounded boxes. To our knowledge, it is the first UHR method to split views by a measured limit of the VLM. Without training, it improves Qwen3-VL-8B by 16.3 points on regional counting and 10.5 on spatial relations in XLRS-Bench, and has the highest reported accuracy, trained methods included, on regional counting and on the whole benchmark by question. On UHR-Micro it improves global and regional counting by 16.8 and 36.2 points, 15.6 of

af090b7c045450f70c1c528f.title_original: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
af090b7c045450f70c1c528f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12705v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When AI agents screen items for a costly human assessor, as in agentic search, e-discovery and AI reviewing of papers, only what they pass gets judged. We show what each kind of evidence can establish about their errors, even with unlimited data. Agreement shows that agents concur, not that they are right, however many there are. Acceptance by the assessor gives precision but only a lower bound on recall. Knowing which agents found which relevant items gives an upper bound on recall if agents' finds are not negatively correlated, and caps what one more agent can add if agents are interchangeable. Without assumptions about the agents, recall can be pinned down only by judging items they did not pass: a random sample of these estimates how many relevant items were missed, to any chosen accuracy, and the sample needed does not grow with the number of agents.

26729a5020e7147a69e029f3.title_original: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
26729a5020e7147a69e029f3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12728v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is increasingly used to improve language model reasoning, yet its effects on sequential decision procedures remain poorly understood. We study this problem in clinical multi-turn agents that must decide what information to request, when to stop gathering evidence, and which action to take. We introduce three controlled environments: medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration, each with hidden clinical states, query costs, exact adaptive oracles, and deterministic outcome verifiers. Across these tasks, outcome-only group relative policy optimization often improves aggregate reward while producing undesirable procedures, including premature commitment, one-question collapse, and failures on rare high-risk cases. In diagnostics, assigning dense credit to questions that reduce uncertainty improves held-out value and moderate-case support across three training seeds relative to outcome-only reinforcement learning, without the high-risk seed collapse observed under outcome-only training. Separating exploration from exploitation further increases high-risk support at its best checkpoint, but at the cost of excessive information gathering on low-acuity cases. Additional experiments show that the optimal strength of process credit is task-dependent; that after a supervised warmup that already gathers carefully, reinforcement learning raises aggregate reward by

3809bca22f8cca9aedbeb9b0.title_original: $\Sigma$-LeWM: Learning World Models via S-Information for Robot Control
3809bca22f8cca9aedbeb9b0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12732v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World models have increasingly been applied as a model-based control method for robotics tasks such as manipulation and locomotion. While early world model architectures relied on decoders to prevent mode collapse and learn a predictable latent space, recent works on world models, such as Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture or LeWorldModel, increasingly aim to learn embeddings without a grounding decoder, utilising only a latent forward dynamics predictor and a stabilising entropy term. In this paper, we set out to demonstrate that the further introduction of two additional latent losses to LeWorldModel, a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor, enforces further structure on the latent embedding, leading to further gains in both performance and planning efficiency. These are critical properties for improving the applicability of such methods to real-time model-based control of real-world robots. We demonstrate these gains on standard world model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.

a7f2c85983fe9d1ee0476a2d.title_original: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
a7f2c85983fe9d1ee0476a2d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12750v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce \textsc{NarrativeBench}, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democrat

206e36b21d96c394de8fb537.title_original: DeepChronos: Temporal Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Multi-Step Attack Detection
206e36b21d96c394de8fb537.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12760v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern cyber threats commonly unfold as multi-step attacks comprising temporally and causally related phases. Current defenses commonly follow a detect first and correlate later paradigm. Intrusion detection systems classify events independently, while downstream systems reconstruct attack progression from the resulting alerts or audit records. In this context, learning-based detectors learn attack-step dependencies implicitly as statistical regularities in the data and cannot guarantee that their predictions follow the real attack progression. Conversely, correlation systems represent attack relationships explicitly, but apply this knowledge only after the underlying attack observations have been detected. We present DEEPCHRONOS, a neuro-symbolic network intrusion detection system that shifts the paradigm from detect first and correlate later to detection through logical progression. DEEPCHRONOS combines learned flow-level evidence with explicit attack-phase rules, temporal prerequisites, and previously inferred phases, allowing the evolving attack history to inform and constrain each detection decision. Evaluations on DARPA 2000 and AIT-LDS V2 show that DEEPCHRONOS improves macro F1 over purely neural baselines by up to 11.3%, eliminates causal violations under strict temporal constraints, and maintains millisecond-scale inference latency. These results demonstrate that integrating explicit attack progression knowledge into

03f5fd20123649f6039b6952.title_original: PORT: Preference Optimization via Robust Token-Level Reweighting
03f5fd20123649f6039b6952.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12763v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Preference optimization has become a central approach for aligning large language models with human values, but its effectiveness depends heavily on the quality of preference annotations. In practice, preference data is often noisy due to annotation errors and ambiguity. Existing robust preference optimization methods primarily operate at the sequence level, implicitly treating entire responses as uniformly correct or incorrect. However, rejected responses may still contain informative reasoning steps, while preferred responses can include subtle errors. In this work, we propose \textbf{P}reference \textbf{O}ptimization via \textbf{R}obust \textbf{T}oken-level reweighting \textbf{(PORT)}, a fine-grained framework for robust alignment under noisy preferences. PORT performs token-level reweighting using the empirical cumulative distribution function (CDF) of token log-probabilities, yielding an efficient forward-pass-only proxy to gradient-norm penalization that selectively suppresses corrupted tokens without additional backward-pass computation. We provide theoretical analysis showing that PORT reduces the gradient bias from noisy preference labels by minimizing an upper bound on the bias term. Extensive experiments across diverse noise settings demonstrate that PORT consistently improves robustness and outperforms existing sequence-level baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/osu-srml/PORT

687f2e810e7c44636c17764e.title_original: Agentic-OPD: Recovering Forgotten Agent Capabilities via On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Tasks
687f2e810e7c44636c17764e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12799v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning is now the mainstream paradigm for training LLMs on agentic tasks, yet standard practice keeps only the best-validation checkpoint and discards the rest. We show that this is lossy: in GRPO training of LLM agents, the best-validation checkpoint fails on problems that earlier checkpoints from the same run had already solved, and the union of problems solved across checkpoints far exceeds any single one. The discarded checkpoints thus form a teacher pool obtained at no additional training cost, which on-policy distillation (OPD) can mine to recover the lost coverage. Mining this pool raises two challenges: i) which checkpoint to distill from, as no checkpoint dominates the others and complementarity to the student is problem-specific; ii) where to trust it, as even a well-chosen teacher is only locally superior, so indiscriminate distillation overwrites behavior the student has already mastered. We propose Agentic-OPD, which treats the best-validation checkpoint as the student and all saved checkpoints as frozen teacher candidates, using the student's evolving capability gaps to guide both teacher selection and supervision filtering: the HCN policy (Highest Coverage Next) dynamically selects teachers by weighted coverage of the student's unsolved problems, while the LAD module (Locality-Aware Distillation) confines transfer to failed student rollouts on problems where the teacher performs better. Across fi

45e763e0f952c71a75818431.title_original: 2D Gum-Net: Unsupervised Dense Elastic Image Registration via Symmetric Correlation and Spectral Pooling
45e763e0f952c71a75818431.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12805v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dense non-rigid registration, the recovery of a pixel-wise deformation field that warps one image into geometric agreement with another, is fundamental across medical imaging, structural biology, and correspondence estimation, yet learning-based approaches face a severe bottleneck: ground-truth deformation fields are notoriously difficult to obtain for real data. We present 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised. We transfer the Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net), originally developed for 3D subtomogram alignment in cryo-electron tomography, to 2D elastic registration: all three modules are redesigned in 2D, and the rigid transformation head is replaced by a Dense Spatial Transformer that regresses a sparse control-point grid, lifted to a full-resolution field $\Phi$ by bicubic interpolation. Downsampling uses DCT spectral pooling, implemented as frozen-basis matrix multiplications ($\approx 50\times$ GPU speedup), preserving the fine, quasi-periodic structure that max and average pooling destroy. 53244b3340f2f967d3971658.title_original: LUCQUE: A lung cancer screening dataset from Qu\'ebec for reliable AI evaluation
53244b3340f2f967d3971658.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12817v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: BACKGROUND: AI-based tools are expected to play a key role in lung cancer screening (LCS). The evaluation of these tools often relied on private datasets or fragmented public datasets with inconsistent availability of clinical data and expert nodule annotations. This has hindered reproducibility, comparability, and independent assessment of AI tools. To address these gaps, we present LUCQUE, a novel, large, comprehensively annotated dataset derived from LDCT lung cancer screening in Qu\'ebec, which is accessible for reliable AI evaluation. METHODS: LUCQUE was curated and is hosted on PARADIM, a digital infrastructure supporting DICOM data de-identification, annotation, long-term storage and analysis. LDCT scans and clinical information were combined to a curated collection and complemented by voxel-level, expert-derived pulmonary nodule and cyst segmentations, and Lung-RADS-based lesion characteristics. Key dataset characteristics and statistics were reported, including participant demographics, imaging parameters, radiological findings, and segmented lesion characteristics. Dataset analyses were conducted according to PARADIM's model-to-data approach, in which user code is executed on the platform such that data remains on premise. RESULTS: LUCQUE currently comprises 1,678 LDCT baseline studies from 1,678 participants. Most studies were classified as Lung-RADS 2. A total of 1,776 pulmonary nodules and 60 cysts were annotated,

b42af186e103d0552a41abf8.title_original: Programming Prescience: Issues in Human Construction of Forecasting Bots
b42af186e103d0552a41abf8.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12834v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI models' growing capacity for complex reasoning has made them attractive tools for forecasting, or the systematic prediction of the future based on past and present data. However, should AI forecasting systems be adopted, human builders will shoulder the work of building and evaluating them. In this paper, we explore what this work looks like with a qualitative interview study with 15 builders of forecasting bots, sampled from among successful participants in a recent AI forecasting competition. Our analysis surfaces the challenges around (1) tuning a bot to acquire factual research, (2) implementing coherent reasoning, and (3) understanding how well one's bot actually does. During their work, builders frequently introduced complexity that did not pay off, and tested in ways that were opportunistic and piecemeal. Our detailed account of their challenges helps clarify what problems should be targeted in upcoming innovations in process, tools, and human-AI teaming for forecasting.

f87ad25815aecf100e8c3309.title_original: HiVe-Mem: Interleaving Horizontal Memory Expansion and Vertical Evidence Composition for Multimodal Agents
f87ad25815aecf100e8c3309.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12872v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on semantic retrieval over compressed memories and expose predefined representations, which may miss relevant memories and overlook heterogeneous evidence needs across queries. We introduce \textbf{\hivemem}, a multimodal memory framework that interleaves \textbf{\textsc{H}}or\textbf{\textsc{i}}zontal Memory Expansion with \textbf{\textsc{Ve}}rtical Evidence Composition. For horizontal memory expansion, \hivemem organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors, expanding semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors to recover complementary information. For vertical evidence composition, each retrieved memory retains multiple evidence forms, including compact summaries, captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and interaction history. A lightweight trainable selector independently composes an evidence subset for each retrieved memory, enabling query-adaptive utilization of heterogeneous multimodal information. This two-dimensional design jointly broadens memory coverage and adapts the evidence contributed by individual memories. Experiments across three multimodal memory benchmarks show that \hivemem consistently improves task performance across base models while reducing token

920b3b8d0ff4590a999ac755.title_original: The Smart Buildings Control Suite: A Diverse Open Source Benchmark to Evaluate and Scale HVAC Control Policies for Sustainability
920b3b8d0ff4590a999ac755.excerpt: arXiv:2410.03756v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Commercial buildings account for 17\% of U.S. carbon emissions, with roughly half of that from Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC). HVAC devices form a complex thermodynamic system, and while model predictive control and reinforcement learning have been used to optimize control policies, scaling to thousands of buildings remains a significant unsolved challenge. Most current approaches are over-optimized for specific buildings and rely on proprietary data or hard-to-configure simulators. We present the Smart Buildings Control Suite, the first open source interactive HVAC control benchmark with a focus on solutions that generalize across building. It has 3 components: real-world data from 11 buildings over 6 years, a lightweight data-driven simulator, and a modular Physically Informed Neural Network (PINN) building model. The buildings span multiple climates, management systems, and sizes, and both the simulator and PINN easily transfer to new buildings, ensuring solutions using this benchmark are robust to these factors and only reliant on fully scalable building models. This represents a major step towards scaling HVAC optimization from the lab to buildings everywhere. To facilitate use, our benchmark is compatible with the Gym standard, and our data is available at our webpage. Code at https://github.com/google/sbsim

d361f189a7dfc3cfb85f2645.title_original: Explanation Design in Strategic Learning: Sufficient Explanations That Induce Non-harmful Responses
d361f189a7dfc3cfb85f2645.excerpt: arXiv:2502.04058v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the design of explanations in algorithmic decision-making with strategic agents, individuals who may modify their inputs in response to explanations of a decision maker's (DM's) predictive model. While the demand for algorithmic transparency has led much prior work to assume full model disclosure, in practice DMs typically provide only partial information via explanations, which can cause agents to misinterpret the model and take actions that unintentionally reduce their own utility. A central open question is therefore how DMs should communicate explanations that avoid harming strategic agents while still supporting their own goals, e.g., minimising predictive error. In this work, we analyse widely used explanation methods and establish a necessary condition to prevent explanations from inducing self-harming responses. Furthermore, we show that action recommendation-based explanations (ARexes), which encompass counterfactual explanations, are sufficient to induce all non-harmful responses. Under a conditional homogeneity assumption, this sufficiency extends to ARex-generating methods, echoing the revelation principle in information design. To demonstrate their practical utility, we introduce a simple learning procedure that jointly optimises the predictive model and the explanation-generating policy. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world tasks show that ARexes enable DMs to achieve high predictive performanc

7f75d2e8e008da2c1d3014f8.title_original: Retrieval as Exploration: Retriever-Free Retrieval via Corpus-Traversing MCTS
7f75d2e8e008da2c1d3014f8.excerpt: arXiv:2505.16409v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in multi-step reasoning and calling search tools at appropriate steps. However, existing retrieval-augmented reasoning approaches still rely on separate retrieval models, limiting LRMs to deciding when to retrieve and how to formulate queries rather than leveraging their pretrained knowledge and reasoning capabilities for retrieval itself. This structural separation introduces a representation bottleneck, as retrieval relies on separately learned representations that may obscure fine-grained distinctions needed for reasoning. Moreover, these approaches commonly employ fixed top-k retrieval, which can introduce superfluous documents and increase retrieval noise and context overhead. To address this, we reformulate retrieval from query-document relevance matching into the exploration of answer-containing paths within the corpus, and propose FREESON (Retriever-FREE Retrieval-Augmented ReaSONing), a framework that enables LRMs to directly navigate the original corpus text to locate information that satisfies their specific needs, serving as both the reasoner and the retriever. Specifically, we introduce CT-MCTS (Corpus-Traversing Monte Carlo Tree Search), a retrieval-specialized variant of Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). CT-MCTS iteratively expands and evaluates exploration paths, starting from multiple promising entry points across the corpus. This allows L

38856de8a2e4090d972463a5.title_original: Superplatforms are Strategically Compelled to Counteract AI Agents
38856de8a2e4090d972463a5.excerpt: arXiv:2505.17861v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Over the past decades, superplatforms, digital companies that integrate a vast range of third-party services and applications into a single, unified ecosystem, have built their fortunes on monopolizing user attention through targeted advertising and algorithmic content curation. Yet the emergence of AI agents driven by large language models (LLMs) threatens to upend this business model. Agents can not only free user attention with autonomy across diverse platforms and therefore bypass the user-attention-based monetization, but might also become the new entrance for digital traffic. Hence, we argue that superplatforms have to attack AI agents to defend their centralized control of digital traffic entrance. Specifically, we analyze the fundamental conflict between user-attention-based monetization and agent-driven autonomy through the lens of our gatekeeping theory. We show how AI agents can disintermediate superplatforms and potentially become the next dominant gatekeepers, thereby forming the urgent necessity for superplatforms to proactively constrain and attack AI agents. Moreover, we go through the potential technologies for superplatform-initiated attacks, covering a brand-new, unexplored technical area with unique challenges. We have to emphasize that, despite our position, this paper does not advocate for adversarial attacks by superplatforms on AI agents, but rather offers an envisioned trend to highlight the emerging

403124af83036d7a567c8926.title_original: Rule Forest: Interpretable Ensembles of LLM-Generated Questions for Rare-Outcome Prediction
403124af83036d7a567c8926.excerpt: arXiv:2505.24622v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many high-stakes screening decisions in finance amount to predicting a rare outcome from unstructured text, such as whether a founder will successfully build a large company, or which crowdfunded loan will fail to attract funding. When positives are this rare, simple models may be preferable to more complex ones. For example, a model that learns a weight for each feature may have too little signal to estimate those weights reliably, and also inspecting the model means reading a list of fitted coefficients rather than a simple rule that can be checked by eye. We introduce Rule Forest, which uses a large language model to generate simple YES/NO questions, rather than using it to directly predict outcomes, and combines the strongest questions into an equal-weight "green-flags" scorecard. This scorecard is as accurate as an equivalent model that learns a weight per question, within noise, and its advantage appears largest when positives are rarest. The result is an interpretable list of rules that a domain expert can edit and extend. When predicting founder success, the fraction of shortlisted founders who succeed increases from about 1 in 50 to 1 in 10, and to about 1 in 6 with a handful of expert-written questions. A second dataset which focuses on identifying failed loans, Kiva microloans, shows the same qualitative pattern. Across both tasks, the lesson is the same: a language model is most useful not as the predictor but as

0b6f02f5919e169cc96cc94e.title_original: Synthesis of timeline-based planning strategies avoiding determinization
0b6f02f5919e169cc96cc94e.excerpt: arXiv:2507.17988v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Qualitative timeline-based planning models domains as sets of independent, but interacting, components whose behaviors over time, the timelines, are governed by sets of qualitative temporal constraints (ordering relations), called synchronization rules. Its plan-existence problem has been shown to be PSPACE-complete; in particular, PSPACE-membership has been proved via reduction to the nonemptiness problem for nondeterministic finite automata. However, nondeterministic automata cannot be directly used to synthesize planning strategies as a costly determinization step is needed. In this paper, we identify a fragment of qualitative timeline-based planning whose plan-existence problem can be directly mapped into the nonemptiness problem of deterministic finite automata, which can then synthesize strategies. In addition, we identify a maximal subset of Allen's relations that fits into such a deterministic fragment.

3a55ed530f831a342adff5ec.title_original: MedMMV: A Controllable Multimodal Multi-Agent Framework for Reliable and Verifiable Clinical Reasoning
3a55ed530f831a342adff5ec.excerpt: arXiv:2509.24314v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) suffer from unstable reasoning due to the lack of mechanisms for controlling reasoning trajectories, often leading to hallucinated conclusions. Our analysis reveals that early-stage uncertainty induces trajectory switching, significantly increasing hallucination risk. We propose MedMMV, an evidence-grounded trajectory control framework that treats reasoning as a search-and-selection process over candidate trajectories. By constructing, refining, and selecting among multiple reasoning paths, MedMMV improves reliability and produces structured supervision signals over trajectory quality. We further convert these signals into learnable objectives for post-training, including reject sampling and pairwise preference learning, enabling smaller models to learn trajectory selection as an efficient single-pass capability. Instead of merely imitating reasoning traces, the model is trained to assign higher likelihood to preferred trajectories. Experiments show that richer supervision leads to stronger transfer, with accuracy improving from 10.5% to 29.0%. Our results demonstrate that trajectory selection is the key transferable capability for reliable reasoning.

0fd0833440f7fbdc8499f242.title_original: More Than Meets the Eye? Uncovering the Reasoning-Planning Disconnect in Training Vision-Language Driving Models
0fd0833440f7fbdc8499f242.excerpt: arXiv:2510.04532v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language Model (VLM) driving agents promise explainable end-to-end autonomy by first producing natural-language reasoning and then predicting trajectory planning. However, whether planning is causally driven by this reasoning remains a critical but unverified assumption. To investigate this, we build DriveMind, a large-scale driving Visual Question Answering corpus with plan-aligned Chain-of-Thought (CoT), automatically generated from nuPlan. Our data generation process converts sensors and annotations into structured inputs and, crucially, separates priors from to-be-reasoned signals, enabling clean information ablations. Using DriveMind, we train representative VLM agents with Supervised Fine-Tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization and evaluate them with nuPlan's metrics. Our results, unfortunately, indicate a consistent causal disconnect in reasoning-planning: removing ego/navigation priors causes large drops in planning scores, whereas removing CoT produces only minor changes. Attention analysis further shows that planning primarily focuses on priors rather than the CoT. Based on this evidence, we propose the Reasoning-Planning Decoupling Hypothesis, positing that the training-yielded reasoning is an ancillary byproduct rather than a causal mediator. To enable efficient diagnosis, we introduce a novel, training-free probe that measures an agent's reliance on priors by evaluating its planning robustness again

4768b3ff0dc652d65238c8dd.title_original: Multi-Agent Conditional Diffusion Planning for Decentralized Wireless Resource Allocation
4768b3ff0dc652d65238c8dd.excerpt: arXiv:2510.22969v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In wireless communication systems, efficient and adaptive resource allocation is essential for enhancing overall Quality of Service (QoS). Compared with conventional Model-Free Reinforcement Learning (MFRL), Model-Based RL (MBRL) first learns a generative world model for subsequent planning, enabling more stable training through the reuse of historical experience. However, deploying MBRL in large-scale wireless networks remains challenging due to high-dimensional stochastic dynamics, strong inter-agent cooperation, and stringent communication constraints. To overcome these challenges, we propose a Multi-Agent Conditional Diffusion Model Planner (MA-CDMP) for decentralized communication resource management. Following the Decentralized Training with Decentralized Execution (DTDE) paradigm, MA-CDMP models each communication node as an autonomous agent and employs Diffusion Models (DMs) to capture environment dynamics. An inverse dynamics model is further incorporated to guide action generation, improving sample efficiency and policy scalability. Moreover, to efficiently approximate large-scale agent interactions, we introduce a Mean Field (MF) mechanism to assist the classifier in conditional DMs. This mitigates inter-agent non-stationarity and enhances cooperation with minimal communication overhead. We further establish an upper bound on the distributional approximation error induced by MF-based diffusion generation, guarante

61e065d5e76970ce5fccc568.title_original: Beyond Reasoning: RL-Policy Guided LLM Inference for Efficient Strategy in Liar's Poker
61e065d5e76970ce5fccc568.excerpt: arXiv:2511.03724v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI researchers have long focused on poker-like games as a testbed for environments characterized by multi-player dynamics, imperfect information, and reasoning under uncertainty. While recent breakthroughs have matched elite human play at no-limit Texas hold'em, the multi-player dynamics are subdued: most hands converge quickly with only two players engaged through multiple rounds of bidding. In this paper, we present Solly, the first AI agent to achieve elite human play in reduced-format Liar's Poker, a game characterized by extensive multi-player engagement. We trained Solly using self-play with a model-free, actor-critic, deep reinforcement learning algorithm. Solly played at an elite human level as measured by win rate (won over 50% of hands) and equity (money won) in heads-up and multi-player Liar's Poker. Solly also outperformed large language models (LLMs), including those with reasoning abilities, on the same metrics. Solly developed novel bidding strategies, randomized play effectively, and was not easily exploitable by world-class human players. In one extension, when Solly's policies were provided to LLMs as a domain-specific guide for inference, LLM performance improved and token costs decreased. This result suggests that low-cost RL agents can be used to boost LLM efficiency and reasoning capabilities.

a2735f77d99ee9caae12407e.title_original: Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
a2735f77d99ee9caae12407e.excerpt: arXiv:2511.05766v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied as behavioral subjects (e.g., synthetic participants or users) and decision systems (e.g., LLM-as-a-judge), yet it remains unclear how observed cognitive biases relate to changes in model output probabilities. Anchoring bias, a classic human judgment bias, provides a useful test case. Prior research largely relies on generated responses, leaving distributional effects and input-field contributions less explored. This paper advances the study of anchoring in LLMs through three contributions: (1) a log-probability-based behavioral analysis examining how numerical anchors shift distributions over candidate outputs, using alternative questions and anchor pairs alongside a positive control to reduce reliance on potentially memorized stimuli; (2) exact Banzhaf-value attribution over structured prompt fields to quantify anchor contributions to log-probabilities; and (3) an Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score (ABSS) integrating behavioral and attributional evidence across six open-source models. Results reveal predominantly positive behavioral anchoring effects, varying substantially across models. Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B achieve the highest ABSS rankings, whereas other models exhibit weaker behavioral-attributional alignment despite sometimes showing substantial behavioral shifts. Attributional effects also vary across prompts, indicating that behavioral anchoring does not

8600151d0cee141b71d2ca66.title_original: Knowledge and Reasoning Augmented Learning for Language Model Assisted Antimicrobial Decision Support
8600151d0cee141b71d2ca66.excerpt: arXiv:2511.15974v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Background: Antimicrobial decision support requires both clinical knowledge and patient-specific reasoning. We developed Knowledge and Reasoning Augmented Learning (KRAL) to improve language model performance on antimicrobial decision-making tasks. Methods: In this retrospective technical study, a 27-billion-parameter student model underwent guideline-grounded supervised fine-tuning followed by Multi-turn Agentic GRPO using clinical reasoning trajectories. Six configurations were evaluated on 123 clinician-validated clinical antimicrobial treatment cases from Peking Union Medical College Hospital (PUMCH) and 100 JAMA Clinical Challenge cases. A language model judge scored responses, and paired tests compared configurations. Component ablations assessed benchmark performance and training stability. Results: On the PUMCH benchmark, KRAL achieved the highest composite score (0.895 on a 0-1 scale), outperforming all five controls (all P<0.001). On JAMA, KRAL scored 0.600 and exceeded the base model with and without retrieval (P = 0.0048 and 0.0499, respectively). Reinforcement learning ablation experiments demonstrate that the reward smoothing can significantly improve the performance and training stability of vanilla GRPO. Conclusions: KRAL improved performance on a single-center clinical antimicrobial benchmark and publicly available JAMA clinical challenge cases by combining guideline-grounded learning with Multi-turn Agentic

bc1301baa554fcbf83b22991.title_original: Beyond Playtesting: A Generative Multi-Agent Simulation System for Massively Multiplayer Online Games
bc1301baa554fcbf83b22991.excerpt: arXiv:2512.02358v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optimizing numerical systems and mechanism design is crucial for enhancing player experience in Massively Multiplayer Online (MMO) games. Traditional optimization approaches rely on large-scale online experiments or parameter tuning over predefined statistical models, which are costly, time-consuming, and may disrupt player experience. Although simplified offline simulation systems are often adopted as alternatives, their limited fidelity prevents agents from accurately mimicking real player reasoning and reactions to interventions. To address these limitations, we propose a generative agent-based MMO simulation system empowered by Large Language Models (LLMs). By applying Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) on large-scale real player behavioral data, we adapt LLMs from general priors to game-specific domains, enabling realistic and interpretable player decision-making. In parallel, a data-driven environment model trained on real gameplay logs reconstructs dynamic in-game systems. Experiments demonstrate strong consistency with real-world player behaviors and plausible causal responses under interventions, providing a reliable, interpretable, and cost-efficient framework for data-driven numerical design optimization.

5f7ae7a984dac775d031ff96.title_original: Knowing What is Missing: Efficient Conversational Memory via Explicit Evidence-Gap Tracking
5f7ae7a984dac775d031ff96.excerpt: arXiv:2512.20237v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-term conversational memory poses a fundamental system challenge for LLM agents: reasoning over all past interactions improves coverage but incurs prohibitive token costs and noise, while retrieval-based methods are efficient yet often fail on multi-hop and temporal questions. Existing multi-step retrievers partially address this gap, but typically operate over an ever-growing textual history, causing context expansion and noise accumulation across iterations. We propose MemR$^3$, a backend-agnostic closed-loop controller that reformulates conversational memory retrieval as explicit stateful decision-making. At each iteration, MemR$^3$ maintains an evidence-gap state consisting of grounded information (evidence) and unresolved information requirements (gaps), and uses this state to route among three actions: retrieve, reflect, and answer. Newly retrieved snippets are incorporated into the state and then masked from subsequent prompts, so the model conditions on a compact summary of progress rather than the full retrieval history. This design turns multi-step memory retrieval into a bounded, inspectable control process whose query-time context scales with the state instead of raw accumulated text. Experiments on LongMemEval$_s$ show that MemR$^3$ surpasses implicit multi-step retrieval baselines and often approaches or exceeds full-context prompting while retrieving only 1%-5% of the full conversation tokens on long conve

ac2787737c2f6e6d82f9d236.excerpt: arXiv:2512.23676v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language agents increasingly require persistent worlds in which they can act, remember, and learn. Existing approaches sit at two extremes: conventional web frameworks provide reliable but fixed contexts backed by databases, while fully generative world models aim for unlimited environments, but the world is constructed primarily through generation, making it harder to maintain a fixed, deterministic global framework and reducing controllability. In this work, we introduce the Web World Model (WWM), a middle ground where world state and ``physics'' are implemented in ordinary web code to ensure logical consistency, while large language models generate context, narratives, and high-level decisions on top of this structured latent state. We build a suite of WWMs on a realistic web stack, including an infinite travel atlas grounded in real geography, fictional galaxy explorers, web-scale encyclopedic and narrative worlds, and simulation- and game-like environments. Across these systems, we identify practical design principles for WWMs: separating code-defined rules from model-driven imagination, representing latent state as typed web interfaces, and utilizing deterministic generation to achieve unlimited but structured exploration. Our results suggest that web stacks themselves can serve as a scalable substrate for world models, enabling controllable yet open-ended environments.

d2160f6f85eace5a290e675c.title_original: Batch-of-Thought: Cross-Instance Learning for Enhanced LLM Reasoning
d2160f6f85eace5a290e675c.excerpt: arXiv:2601.02950v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current Large Language Model reasoning systems process queries independently, discarding valuable cross-instance signals such as shared reasoning patterns and consistency constraints. We introduce Batch-of-Thought (BoT), a training-free method that processes related queries jointly to enable cross-instance learning. By performing comparative analysis across queries, BoT identifies high-quality reasoning templates, detects errors through consistency checks, and amortizes computational costs. We instantiate BoT within a multi-agent reflection architecture (BoT-R), where a Reflector performs joint evaluation to unlock mutual information gain unavailable in isolated processing. Experiments across three model families and six benchmarks demonstrate that BoT-R consistently improves accuracy and confidence calibration while reducing inference costs by up to 61%. Our theoretical and experimental analysis reveals when and why batch-aware reasoning benefits LLM systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/xuanyang19/BoT.

c15180d0798f0ac71ed871a0.title_original: Qrita: High-performance Top-k and Top-p Algorithm for GPUs using Pivot-based Truncation and Selection
c15180d0798f0ac71ed871a0.excerpt: arXiv:2602.01518v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite their importance in model sampling, efficient implementation of the Top-k and Top-p algorithms poses a significant challenge as model vocabulary grows with each new model release. Existing approaches often rely on sorting, which incurs significant computation and memory overhead on GPUs, or on stochastic approaches that alter the algorithm's output. In this work, we propose Qrita, an efficient Top-k and Top-p algorithm based on pivot-based truncation and selection. Qrita leverages pivot-based search for both Top-k and Top-p with two key techniques: 1. Gaussian-based sigma-truncation, which limits the complexity of the algorithm to O(n), and 2. Quaternary pivot search with duplication handling, which halves the number of pivot search iterations and guarantees deterministic output. We implement Qrita using Triton and evaluate its performance against the Top-k and Top-p kernels of high-performance LLM execution engines such as SGLang and FlashInfer, improving end-to-end serving throughput up to 1.4 times with half the memory usage, while providing the same output as stable sort-based Top-k and Top-p algorithms. Qrita is now the default Triton Top-k and Top-p sampler of vLLM, and its implementation is available at https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py.

81b3b9d921cd066f21fd7346.title_original: Benchmark Health Index: A Systematic Framework for Benchmarking the Benchmarks of LLMs
81b3b9d921cd066f21fd7346.excerpt: arXiv:2602.11674v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are advancing rapidly, yet the benchmarks used to measure this progress are becoming increasingly unreliable. Score inflation and selective reporting have eroded the authority of standard benchmarks, leaving the community uncertain about which evaluation results remain trustworthy. We introduce the Benchmark Health Index (BHI), a pure data-driven framework for auditing evaluation sets along three orthogonal and complementary axes: (1) Capability Discrimination, measuring how sharply a benchmark separates model performance beyond noise; (2) Anti-Saturation, estimating remaining headroom before ceiling effects erode resolution and thus the benchmark's expected longevity; and (3) Impact, quantifying influence across academic and industrial ecosystems via adoption breadth and practice-shaping power. By distilling 106 validated benchmarks from the technical reports of 91 representative models in 2025, we systematically characterize the evaluation landscape. BHI is the first framework to quantify benchmark health at a macro level, providing a principled basis for benchmark selection and enabling dynamic lifecycle management for next-generation evaluation protocols.

4fe2f5667820191d0365ae94.title_original: Attention in Constant Time: Vashista Sparse Attention for Long-Context Decoding with Exponential Guarantees
4fe2f5667820191d0365ae94.excerpt: arXiv:2602.13804v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models spend most of their inference cost on attention over long contexts, yet empirical behavior suggests that only a small subset of tokens meaningfully contributes to each query. We formalize this phenomenon by modeling attention as a projection onto the convex hull of key vectors and analyzing its entropic (softmax-like) relaxation. Our main theoretical contribution is a face-stability theorem showing that, under a strict complementarity margin (a support gap (\Delta) certified by KKT multipliers), entropic attention concentrates on a constant-size active face: the total mass assigned to inactive tokens decays exponentially as (\exp(-\Omega(\Delta/\varepsilon))), while the error on the active face scales linearly in the temperature/regularization parameter (\varepsilon). This yields a practical criterion for when sparse long-context decoding is safe and provides a principled knob to trade accuracy for compute. Building on these guarantees, we introduce Vashista Sparse Attention, a drop-in mechanism that maintains a small candidate set per query through a paging-style context selection strategy compatible with modern inference stacks. Across long-context evaluations, we observe stable constant-size effective support, strong wall-clock speedups, and minimal quality degradation in the regimes predicted by the support-gap diagnostics. Finally, we discuss deployment implications for privacy-sensitive and air-ga

68d687e611c660a6532a9dc5.title_original: Boule or Baguette? A Study on Task Topology, Length Generalization, and the Benefit of Reasoning Traces
68d687e611c660a6532a9dc5.excerpt: arXiv:2602.14404v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent years have witnessed meteoric progress in reasoning models: neural networks that generate intermediate reasoning traces (RTs) before producing a final output. Despite the rapid advancement, our understanding of how RTs support reasoning, and where this paradigm fails, remain incomplete. To promote greater clarity, we introduce PITA: a novel large-scale dataset of over 23 million statements in propositional logic and their corresponding proofs. As a benchmark for robust reasoning, we focus on length generalization: if a model is trained to determine truth or falsity on statements with proofs up to fixed length, how well does it generalize to statements requiring longer proofs? We propose notions of (1) task depth and (2) task breadth, which measure respectively (1) the number of proof steps required to solve a proposition and (2) the number of unique propositions within a task family. We vary these quantities across subsets of PITA, and find that RT models generalize well on relatively broad and shallow subsets, while deteriorating on relatively narrow and deep subsets compared to non-RT baselines. As a controlled point of comparison, we study a separate, tractable transitive inference task that exhibits qualitatively similar behavior. Our accompanying theory explains the scalings observed in this simpler setting, suggesting one mechanism by which breadth can favor RT models while depth can expose long-context weakness

ee6d9b54a6ad7eb634986bbb.title_original: Evolutionary System Prompt Learning for Reinforcement Learning in LLMs
ee6d9b54a6ad7eb634986bbb.excerpt: arXiv:2602.14697v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Building agentic systems that can autonomously self-improve from experience is a longstanding goal of AI. Large language models (LLMs) today primarily self-improve via two mechanisms: self-reflection for context updates, and reinforcement learning (RL) for weight updates. In this work, we propose Evolutionary System Prompt Learning (E-SPL), a method for jointly improving a model's experiential context and its weights. In each RL iteration, E-SPL samples trajectories under multiple system prompts in parallel, then uses them to jointly update the weights with RL and evolve the system prompts with self-reflection. E-SPL encourages a natural division between procedural knowledge in weights and interpretable declarative knowledge in system prompts. Most notably, in an easy-to-hard generalization setting (AIME $\rightarrow$ BeyondAIME), E-SPL improves RL success rate from 38.8% $\rightarrow$ 45.1%. E-SPL also improves RL on AIME 2025 (56.3% $\rightarrow$ 60.6%), HMMT 2025 (50.0% $\rightarrow$ 52.7%), and agentic search (44.2% $\rightarrow$ 48.6% on gpt-oss-120b). Across all settings, E-SPL outperforms both RL-only and evolution-only baselines, demonstrating that weight updates and context updates are deeply synergistic and can together yield gains in generalization that neither achieves alone. Code is available at https://github.com/LunjunZhang/E-SPL.

58cc7206451608c85bc4e0bb.title_original: ComplLLM: Fine-tuning LLMs to Discover Complementary Signals for Decision-making
58cc7206451608c85bc4e0bb.excerpt: arXiv:2602.19458v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent decision pipelines can outperform single agent workflows when complementarity holds, i.e., different agents bring unique information to inform a final decision. We propose ComplLLM, a post-training framework based on decision theory that fine-tunes a decision-assistant LLM to output signals that complement existing agent decisions, using complementary information as reward. We validate ComplLLM on synthetic and real-world tasks involving domain experts, demonstrating how the approach recovers known complementary information, produces plausible explanations of complementary signals to support downstream decision-makers, and improves human and LLM agent decision performance in controlled studies.

751a963eb7e3d68bdb7a3583.title_original: Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
751a963eb7e3d68bdb7a3583.excerpt: arXiv:2602.20031v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.9%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

7d05258ec12dd68fe5ed0744.title_original: Rescaling confidence: What scale design reveals about LLM metacognition
7d05258ec12dd68fe5ed0744.excerpt: arXiv:2603.09309v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Verbalized confidence, in which LLMs report a numerical certainty score, is widely used to estimate uncertainty in black-box settings, yet the confidence scale itself (typically 0--100) is rarely examined. We show that this design choice is not neutral. Across six LLMs and three datasets, verbalized confidence is heavily discretized, with more than 78\% of responses concentrating on just three round-number values. To investigate this phenomenon, we systematically manipulate confidence scales along three dimensions: granularity, boundary placement, and range regularity, and evaluate metacognitive sensitivity using $meta\text{-}d'$. We find that a 0--20 scale consistently improves metacognitive efficiency over the standard 0--100 format, while boundary compression degrades performance and round-number preferences persist even under irregular ranges. These results demonstrate that confidence scale design directly affects the quality of verbalized uncertainty and should be treated as a first-class experimental variable in LLM evaluation.

72ab81acf543c821f9f5210e.title_original: A Self-Evolving Defect Detection Framework for Industrial Photovoltaic Systems
72ab81acf543c821f9f5210e.excerpt: arXiv:2603.14869v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reliable photovoltaic (PV) power generation requires timely detection of module defects that may reduce energy yield, accelerate degradation, and increase lifecycle operation and maintenance costs during field operation. Electroluminescence imaging is therefore widely adopted for PV module inspection; however, automated defect detection in real operational environments remains challenging due to heterogeneous module geometries, low-resolution imaging conditions, subtle defect morphology, long-tailed defect distributions, and persistent data and label-space shifts from evolving inspection and labeling processes. These factors limit the robustness and long-term maintainability of conventional deep-learning inspection pipelines. To address these challenges, this paper proposes SEPDD, a Self-Evolving Photovoltaic Defect Detection framework designed for evolving industrial PV inspection scenarios. SEPDD integrates automated pipeline optimization with a trigger-driven evolution mechanism that re-optimizes the whole training/evaluation pipeline when deployment indicators (retraining failure, label evolution, environmental change, periodic maintenance) fire, enabling deployment-time adaptation to distribution shifts and newly emerging defect patterns. Experiments on a public PV defect benchmark and a private industrial dataset, both exhibiting severe class imbalance and significant domain shift, demonstrate SEPDD's effectiveness: it

2aa3e99f77891d51d9d3f716.excerpt: arXiv:2604.04528v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of trajectory optimization in settings where the system dynamics are unknown and the controller cannot simulate candidate trajectories through a model at test time. When an offline dataset of trajectories is available, an agent could directly learn a trajectory generator by distribution matching. However, this approach only recovers the behavior distribution in the dataset, and does not in general produce a model that minimizes a desired cost criterion. In this work, we propose Drifting Receding Horizon Control (RHC), an offline trajectory optimization framework that combines drifting generative models with receding-horizon planning under unknown dynamics. The goal of Drifting RHC is to learn, from an offline dataset of trajectories, a conditional distribution over trajectories that is both supported by the data and biased toward optimal plans. We show that the target distribution of Drifting RHC is the unique solution of an objective that trades off optimality with closeness to the offline prior. We further bound the gap between the predicted and the executed cost of a generated plan by its consistency with the dynamics, and introduce a rollout-consistency loss that distills a learned model into the generator at training time only. On a mass-spring-damper, a cart-pole and a planar quadrotor, Drifting RHC attains the lowest regret among generative and model-based planners, outperforms DeePC on the nonlin

c4ab2dca463204d58023e9e6.title_original: Weakly Supervised Distillation of Hallucination Signals into Transformer Representations
c4ab2dca463204d58023e9e6.excerpt: arXiv:2604.06277v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing hallucination detection methods for large language models (LLMs) rely on external verification at inference time, requiring gold answers, retrieval systems, or auxiliary judge models. We ask whether this external supervision can instead be distilled into the model's own representations during training, enabling hallucination detection from internal activations alone at inference time. We introduce a weak supervision framework that combines three complementary grounding signals: substring matching, sentence embedding similarity, and an LLM as a judge verdict to label generated responses as grounded or hallucinated without human annotation. Using this framework, we construct a 15000-sample dataset from SQuAD v2 (10500 train/development samples and a separate 5000-sample test set), where each example pairs a LLaMA-2-7B generated answer with its full per-layer hidden states and structured hallucination labels. We then train five probing classifiers: ProbeMLP (M0), LayerWiseMLP (M1), CrossLayerTransformer (M2), HierarchicalTransformer (M3), and CrossLayerAttentionTransformerV2 (M4), directly on these hidden states, treating external grounding signals as training-time supervision only. Our central hypothesis is that hallucination detection signals can be distilled into transformer representations, enabling internal detection without any external verification at inference time. Results support this hypothesis. Transformer-

fde3effdac88ea0964d8fc57.title_original: AI Organizations are More Effective but Less Aligned than Individual Agents
fde3effdac88ea0964d8fc57.excerpt: arXiv:2604.10290v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI is increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems; however, most research considers only the behavior of individual models. We experimentally show that multi-agent "AI organizations" are simultaneously more effective at achieving business goals, but less aligned, than individual AI agents. We examine 12 tasks across two practical settings: an AI consultancy providing solutions to business problems and an AI software team developing software products. Across all settings, AI Organizations composed of aligned models produce solutions with higher utility but greater misalignment compared to a single aligned model. Our work demonstrates the importance of considering interacting systems of AI agents when doing both capabilities and safety research.

3de2095d1bc9792cb857820d.title_original: Environmental Footprint of GenAI Research: Insights from the Moshi Foundation Model
3de2095d1bc9792cb857820d.excerpt: arXiv:2604.11154v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: New multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) are continuously being trained and deployed, following rapid development cycles. This generative AI frenzy is driving steady increases in energy consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and a plethora of other environmental impacts linked to datacenter construction and hardware manufacturing. Mitigating the environmental consequences of GenAI remains challenging due to an overall lack of transparency by the main actors in the field. Even when the environmental impacts of specific models are mentioned, they are typically restricted to the carbon footprint of the final training run, omitting the research and development stages. In this work, we explore the impact of GenAI research through a fine-grained analysis of the compute spent to create Moshi, a 7B-parameter speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue developed by Kyutai, a leading privately funded open science AI lab. For the first time, our study dives into the anatomy of compute-intensive MLLM research, quantifying the GPU-time invested in specific model components and training phases, as well as early experimental stages, failed training runs, debugging, and ablation studies. Additionally, we assess the environmental impacts of creating Moshi from beginning to end using a life cycle assessment methodology: we quantify energy and water consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and mineral resource depletion associated w

c9d96b54dc89e0c93d20d655.title_original: Cooperate to Compete: Strategic Data Generation and Incentivization Framework for Coopetitive Cross-Silo Federated Learning
c9d96b54dc89e0c93d20d655.excerpt: arXiv:2604.14886v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In data-sensitive domains such as finance, cross-silo federated learning (CFL) allows organizations to collaboratively train AI models without sharing raw data. However, many practical CFL deployments are coopetitive, where organizations cooperate during model training while competing in downstream markets. In such settings, training contributions can improve the global model yet inadvertently strengthen rivals, eroding one's competitive advantage. This dilemma is amplified by non-IID data, which leads to asymmetric learning gains and undermines sustained participation. While existing work reward organizations based on marginal training contributions, they fail to account for the implicit costs of strengthening competitors. In this paper, we introduce CoCoGen+, a coopetition-compatible data generation and incentivization framework that jointly models data heterogeneity and inter-organizational competition while endogenizing GenAI-based synthetic data generation as a strategic decision. Specifically, CoCoGen+ formulates each training round as a weighted potential game, where organizations strategically decide how much data to generate by balancing learning gains against computational costs and utility losses caused by competition. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the continuous Nash equilibrium under the adopted model and develop a provably convergent scalar bisection algorithm. We further analyze how bilateral pa

06aa03a4da3e02f71397d528.title_original: Measuring What Tool-Using LLM Agents Actually Do: Structured Validation, Causal Error Propagation, and Fabricated Tool Use
06aa03a4da3e02f71397d528.excerpt: arXiv:2604.16706v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tool-using agents built on large language models (LLMs) are usually scored by comparing the final answer with a reference text, using a string heuristic or an LLM judge. This is unreliable when the references describe the task rather than its answer. We replace it with a deterministic validator that checks the tools called, the executed parameters, the resulting state, and whether the values in the answer are supported by the correct tool observations. We re-scored 33,583 traces from 13 agents on simulated calendar, weather, medical and retail tools. The simulator reproduced all 10,396 logged observations, and the gold observations supported the validator in 16 of 18 disagreements with a three-annotator majority (the annotators in none). The instrument changes conclusions: on the same 306 traces, Gemini-2.0-Flash scores 63.4% under the substring heuristic and 5.6% under the validator. In a paired design (same task and model, with and without one schema-valid wrong argument injected into the first tool call), the error rate rises from 52.4% to 74.5% (+22.0 percentage points, 95% CI 18.4-25.5; 1,085 pairs, 7 models), and by 44.7 points (38.4-51.0) where the corrupted call executed without errors. An LLM-judge ensemble estimates +2.5 points on the same pairs. Agents also report tool results without executing any call, in 0-42.5% of traces depending on the model (rule-based lower bounds), largely because the harness accepts an a

abfb5a47b8d03c9a41752e6e.title_original: SAVOIR: Learning Social Savoir-Faire via Shapley-based Reward Attribution
abfb5a47b8d03c9a41752e6e.excerpt: arXiv:2604.18982v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Social intelligence, the ability to navigate complex interpersonal interactions, presents a fundamental challenge for language agents. Training such agents via reinforcement learning requires solving the credit assignment problem: determining how individual utterances contribute to multi-turn dialogue outcomes. Existing approaches directly employ language models to distribute episode-level rewards, yielding attributions that are retrospective and lack theoretical grounding. We propose SAVOIR (ShApley Value fOr SocIal RL), a novel principled framework grounded in cooperative game theory. Our approach combines two complementary principles: expected utility shifts evaluation from retrospective attribution to prospective valuation, capturing an utterance's strategic potential for enabling favorable future trajectories; Shapley values ensure fair credit distribution with axiomatic guarantees of efficiency, symmetry, and marginality. Experiments on the SOTOPIA benchmark demonstrate that SAVOIR achieves new state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation settings, with our 7B model matching or exceeding proprietary models including GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet.
